editorials.title: Renting a friend, toilet paper tariffs, and more...
editorials.passage:
There are few things more American than using an unreasonable amount of toilet paper.

In fact, the average American goes through about 141 rolls a year, making the US the world's biggest toilet paper consumer despite having only around 4% of the global population. And now, thanks to the latest US-Canada trade war, even that very American habit could get a little more expensive.

You see, Canada has threatened to slap tariffs of up to 50% on American paper products starting in September, in retaliation for the tariffs imposed by the US. And while most toilet paper sold in America is made in America, much of what goes into making it comes from Canada.

This is because Canada is home to large forests and a well-established pulp and paper industry, so American manufacturers have spent decades building supply chains around relatively cheap Canadian raw materials.

A tree might be grown in Canada, turned into pulp there, shipped across the border, processed by an American manufacturer, and eventually end up sitting on a shelf at Costco.

This is why a tariff doesn't need to hit the “final product” for consumers to feel it. And if the cost of the raw material goes up, manufacturers have two choices:

And unlike napkins, toilet paper isn't exactly something consumers can easily decide to stop buying until prices come down.

The irony here is that the most vulnerable products aren't necessarily the glamorous ones. It's the things that sit unnoticed in our homes until their prices suddenly change.

So perhaps the strangest realisation from this trade war is that the tariffs America imposes may ultimately hit much closer to people's homes, or, in this case, slightly below it. And if this continues, Americans might just finally start using a jet spray.

What caught our eye this week 👀

The companionship economy

A screenshot went viral in India last month showing a "rent me for a day" rate card. Coffee date, ₹1,500. Family meeting, ₹3,000. Weekend getaway, ₹10,000. And even after a lot of back and forth, nobody could verify if the person behind it was even real.

Meanwhile, in Russia, this isn't a hoax at all. Men are running actual classified ads offering to show up at your barbecue and keep you company for $13 to $65, no strings attached.

So what's actually going on here?

Well, there's a term for it: the companionship economy.

And it's not just some weird dude behind his laptop in his mom’s basement. AI is joining in, too. Just the AI companionship economy is projected to grow from $30 million to $150 billion globally by 2030. But why would anyone pay a stranger, let alone an AI chatbot, for something friends are supposed to do for free?

Well, behavioral economist Dan Ariely has an answer for this, and it comes down to something he calls ‘social’ norms versus ‘market’ norms.

He argues that we live by two completely different rulebooks. Ask a friend to help you move, and they'll show up happily. Offer to pay them for it, and you've just insulted them. This is because social exchanges run on goodwill and unspoken reciprocity. However, if you have to hire packers and movers, you have to discuss the terms upfront. Because that’s how market exchanges work. And these two don't mix well.

But by paying a total stranger, you get the best of both worlds. It keeps expectations clear and leaves zero obligation on either side.

There's a second piece of psychology at play too. Cornell researcher Vanessa Bohns has spent years studying why people don't just ask their friends for company or help in the first place. We're all walking around assuming rejection is more likely than it is, and that fear alone stops a lot of people from ever reaching out. And her findings are almost embarrassing: we consistently underestimate how willing other people are to say yes.

But when you’re paying for a service, the answer is almost always yes, whether it is a person or an AI service.

And this isn’t some distant prediction. Take Replika. It lets users create an AI friend, mentor, or even a romantic partner. But features that make the relationship feel more real, such as romantic conversations, voice calls, selfies, and better memory, sit behind paid subscriptions.

Or take ElliQ, a tabletop AI companion designed for older adults. It chats with them, plays games, offers reminders, and simply keeps them company for all for a monthly fee (plus the device cost, of course).

So people are buying not merely a conversation, but attention and the guarantee that someone (or something) will always answer.

editorials.title: .Spycam specs
editorials.passage:
A legal notice to Meta and an Instagram user, issued by a man in Delhi, over a video allegedly recorded without his knowledge using Meta smart glasses should set off alarm bells in India. The incident points to the possibility of ordinary-looking spectacles becoming a tool for covert recording, humiliation, harassment and even sexual exploitation.

The risk is no longer just theory. Reports from Sweden reveal that contractors working for Meta’s data-annotation partner said they had seen recordings captured by the glasses in deeply private situations. Meta has said that the material remains on the device unless users share it with Meta or others, and that safeguards are used when shared material is reviewed. But the fact remains — and this is indefensible — that once a camera is embedded in something that looks like an ordinary pair of spectacles, the person being filmed may have no idea that a recording is taking place. Worse, the recording indicator is hardly an impregnable safeguard. Reports have found that the LED can be tampered with.

Many countries are already taking the threat seriously. Texas has opened an investigation into Meta’s glasses over concerns including recordings, facial data and the effectiveness of the recording indicator. Germany has seen a criminal complaint filed against Meta and others over alleged covert filming; its regulator has also warned about the privacy risks of smart glasses. In Britain, courts have barred their use in courtrooms, while cinemas are restricting them. Sweden’s data-protection authority has separately issued guidance warning users about the ease of discreet filming. The argument for allowing the glasses is not particularly compelling anyway for the average consumer. Most of their headline features including taking photographs, listening to music, making calls, asking an AI assistant questions or translating text, are conveniences that smartphones and earbuds already provide. The privacy risk, however, is significant.

While a smartphone camera usually has to be pointed at someone, a pair of glasses can record while the wearer appears to be doing nothing at all. In the Indian context, monitoring millions of users and detecting covert recording is inherently difficult. By the time a victim discovers a recording, it may already have been uploaded and widely circulated. Worse, cheaper versions of smart glasses are flooding the Indian market enabling easy proliferation. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection framework also remains under phased implementation, with key provisions not taking effect until 2027. Its headline penalties, up to ₹250 crore for some breaches, may not be substantial compared to the damage the glasses can do. There may be select uses that justify making the technology available. For the visually impaired, hands-free AI, visual descriptions and assistance can be genuinely transformative. If such benefits are demonstrated, policymakers could permit those applications with strict guardrails. But for everyone else, policymakers should move quickly to stop the sale of this device in the country.

Published on August 28, 2026

editorials.title: In women’s Hockey World Cup, fifth place and  plenty to build on for India
editorials.passage:
A fifth place may not carry the sheen of a medal. But India has returned from the Women’s Hockey World Cup in the Netherlands and Belgium with something almost as significant: Proof that the team is among the game’s best again. The team’s best finish since 1974 came after a disastrous four-year stretch in which the promise of fourth place at the Tokyo Olympics gave way to missed opportunities and poor results. The team failed to qualify for the Paris Olympics, lost its Pro League status and was beaten by China in the Asia Cup final last year. Against that backdrop, holding China, England and Australia, losing only once in six matches and then beating world No. 5 Germany 3-1 marks a remarkable turnaround.

In three weeks, India will travel to Japan for the Asian Games with a legitimate shot at their first-ever gold. China remain the team to beat, but the World Cup showed that the gap between the two isn’t insurmountable. India matched them in their group-stage draw and, with a defence that stood firm against some of the world’s strongest attacks and a young generation gaining confidence, the team has every reason to believe it can overturn last year’s Asia Cup disappointment.

Hockey India cannot, however, afford to treat this as a feel-good moment. Reports that the Women’s Hockey India League could be in trouble are particularly alarming, with captain Savita Punia publicly urging authorities to ensure its continuation. The women have now shown twice — first at the Tokyo Olympics and now again at the World Cup — that they can go toe-to-toe with the best. The task now is to ensure that support grows.

editorials.title: Unkind cuts: On the Telangana and Karnataka electoral rolls
editorials.passage:
The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process being conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI) is increasingly leading to a clear case of disenfranchisement in several parts of India. Marauding on after a judgment by the Supreme Court of India allowed it to proceed, the SIR has now struck out a fifth of the names from the electoral rolls in Telangana and Karnataka — nearly 22% and 19.5% respectively — and among the highest in the country. The cuts are steepest in their capital cities — five constituencies in Bengaluru have lost more than half of their electors while nine of Hyderabad’s 15 have seen deletions of more than 40%. Cuts of this kind cannot simply be a trimming of bloated rolls at the margins. If they are accurate, the ECI’s own summary revision processes were yielding bloated rolls in recent elections, and doing so in the very places with high net in-migration from the rest of India. And if the deletions are to be justified, those struck off the rolls must have left the States — a move within Karnataka or Telangana would only relocate a voter’s name on the same State roll, not remove it altogether. Yet, this is neither borne out by recent survey data nor by the government’s own population estimates.

During the Bihar SIR, the Court asked why political parties had filed so few objections, seeking inclusion of wrongly deleted names; that question might hold true for the Southern States as well. A plausible reason could be that the voter id is useful to a citizen only once in a few years, leading to less alacrity on their part. This may explain why a process that puts the onus on electors yields cuts of this scale. Meanwhile, proving a smoking gun in the data is difficult because of the ECI’s opacity. It has not published the elector-to-population ratio for any State so far during the revision even though doing so is mandatory and is the only test of under-enrolment. The Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer has not even bothered to release a gender-wise breakdown of the deletions, instead scattering the lists across several Google Drive links without the old booth numbers, making verification arduous. The outcome of such shoddiness is visible in West Bengal, where the ECI’s dubious “logical discrepancy” process disenfranchised lakhs of electors, forcing them to seek redress before tribunals set up under the aegis of the Court. Months after the elections, records obtained under a Right to Information request show that barely 82,000 of the nearly 38 lakh appeals before the 19 tribunals have been decided, with more than 90% of those decisions favouring electors seeking restoration. The ECI — an institution once envied even by wealthier democracies for bringing large numbers of Indians to the polling booth — is now an obstacle to universal adult franchise.

editorials.title: The dilemma in treating defamation as an offence
editorials.passage:
A particular “crime” and the punishment laid down for it in India are the subject of this column today. As well as an associated dilemma.

The issue in question is defamation, and more specifically, insults offered by political persons to other political persons, and by anyone, wittingly or unwittingly, to the State and its symbols. The dilemma is this: We need to curb this, but we also need to be wary of how this curbing can have a political dimension. Together, these two situations constitute a problem in themselves. I have no solutions to offer for this problem, only ruminations and the busy reader may disengage right here, and only read on if interested.

Let us take the act first. Using hurtful and insulting words to make the targeted person feel shocked and humiliated is one of humankind’s timeless weapons of belligerence. In India, we have used it with abandon. What in Hindi is called gaali-galauch, has been, down the centuries, deployed to cause a person, and his or her self-respect, hurt. Defamation is only the legal name for the old practice. The laws of libel or defamation in India as elsewhere are designed to curb the pernicious practice and protect victims of it. Typically, gaali-type oral defamation does not get carried to courts — the process is too intimidating. But when the persons concerned are famous, and the insult has been hurled in the public domain, the matter gets to be known widely and can lead to the courts’ doors being knocked on. This has happened in recent months, noticeably.

Of such insults, the most hurtful are those that bring in the mothers and female relatives of the one being taunted. Even as the nation is engaged in reverencing the National Song with its invocation of Mother India, sons of Mother India, in the course of arguments or brawls, have no difficulty insulting mothers of fellow Indians. None at all. Or the daughters of Mother India.

The insult is spat out, horror results, apologies are demanded, the charge is denied or ascribed to provocation, the demand gets reiterated, and the episode is magnified. Social media blares: “What have we come to?” The fact is we have come to no place that we were not already in. The vocabularies of our great languages have, since God knows when, had to endure an unprinted supplement of lewd swear words. The supplement has yet another sub-supplement, involving the genitalia of the female of our species. This is a hideous truth about our vocabularies of abuse; let prudishness not deny it, nor primness shy from it. That the world’s other languages may be no different in this, is certainly no consolation.

Like any reader of this column, I am nauseated by the phenomenon of gaali-galauch and its manifestation in the public arena. Bringing in mothers and sisters and wives directly and through innuendos is simply hideous. Anyone with a sense of decency would want to see it put down. But how should that be done?

Penology is influenced by precedents and conventions. So, let us see what Kautilya’s Arthashastra, written about 2,400 years ago, says on the subject. This grand text is, in its own way, a penal code, listing and defining crimes and prescribing penalties for a range of criminal acts for the guidance of the Mauryan State. Kautilya, better known as Chanakya, goes in great detail into the nature and variety of defamatory acts. I have not enough Sanskrit to read the original, but have gathered from the late Indian diplomat LN Rangarajan’s stunning translation into English (Penguin Classics, 1992, p. 436) that the Mauryan-era mastermind divided defamation into simple defamation and aggravated defamation. The latter category included as a crime “insulting” , in the following order : “one’s mother, father, brother, teacher or an ascetic”. And the punishment he laid down for such an offence was “cutting off the tongue”. Ouch!

This punishment was the same as that for “insulting the king; divulging State secrets; spreading false rumours [about the king]”. Cutting off the tongue, in all these cases.

So, in the Mauryan State, Kautilya equated insulting a mother with insulting a guru or the sovereign himself, no less. One part of me — the part that is disgusted by the phenomenon of gaali-galauch — says, “Bravo, Kautilya! Bravo for equating the mother with the sovereign.” The king says, “Anyone insulting a mother in my realm, insults me.” Or almost that. A tongue that insults the king will get cut off, a tongue that insults a mother will, too. Or almost that.

Loose tongues in today’s India will thank God they are not in Mauryan India. Ancient India had its norms; we are, 2,000 years later, not bound by that manner of punishment, thank God. But I would say this: For insults that bring in matrimony, maternity, sorority, a wholly civilised, non-corporal, and appealable equivalent of the barbaric punishment prescribed by Kautilya would not be a bad thing.

Another part of me would immediately say, “Hold it! Any punishment code has to have a common definitional base point on the mens rea (the accused’s intent) and on the objective of the punishment (retribution, prevention, or reform).

That is where the question boils down to one word: disrespect. The onus for determining the disrespect-quotient in a charge of defamation lies on the Courts and is indeed onerous. Why, their own orders could themselves come up for the same determination in a higher court!

To sum up: Insulting and humiliating through words or action, an old and ugly trait, is now particularly active in the public, specifically, political arena where maternity-based and matrimony-related swear words, insinuations, and innuendos are traded by politicians and their supporters. Individual insults suffer little or no risk of judicial miscarriage but when the plaintiff is a political entity, including the State, the situation gets complicated.

Can political defamation be checked without political score-settling? This is a dilemma. And it is not an ordinary one. Seemingly right and good things are done with dubious intentions, and patently wrong and bad steps are taken wearing noiseless and soft footwear.

This is where statespersons in office like Presidents Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, R Venkataraman and KR Narayanan are missed. They would have consulted the country’s Prime Minister and law minister and even held informal soundings with them. They were thought-partners with the people. And apart from them, the country had tribunes such as Bhimrao Ambedkar, C Rajagopalachari, Muthulakshmi Reddy, Jayaprakash Narayan, Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, Acharya and Sucheta Kripalani, and VR Krishna Iyer. That word — tribune — has a meaning we need to recall. In ancient Rome, a tribune was an elected official who protected the common people (plebeians) from the ruling class (patricians).

Whether as elected representatives or otherwise, they and others like them were there in the public proscenium to counsel and to guide us through existential crises affecting our nationhood.

Nostalgia for them and for those times, I know, is no cure for the specific malaise described here. But awareness of the diagnosis and of the absence of medication can perhaps be the beginning of change. We need tribunes, men and women of stature, esteemed in their persons and for values who can chasten society and check the State. The judiciary, overburdened as it is, can only act on matters before it. Tribunes can choose their matters. The matters are many; tribunes few if any.

Gopalkrishna Gandhi is a student of modern Indian history and the author of The Undying Light: A Personal History of Independent India. The views expressed are personal

editorials.title: political donations: Labour should curb the power of big money
editorials.passage:
On the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham told a democracy activist that he favoured a political donations cap of around £500,000 and wanted it reduced over time. His government is now resisting amendments that would move in precisely that direction. Mr Burnham was right in May. He is wrong now. It is difficult to argue that restricting a single person to giving half a million pounds a year to a political party would damage democracy. Such a cap would only affect the mega-rich. Reducing the cap would force parties to wean themselves off the present regime that allows the rich too much say.

There are two contra arguments swilling around Labour. The first is that there should be room for wealthy, progressive donors – whose cash helps rebut claims that Labour is in the pocket of the trade unions. The second is the warning from unions that a cap could undermine their ability to contribute to the Labour party.

Neither of these arguments holds much water. Whatever benefit Labour might derive from rich friends is dwarfed by the wider damage caused by parties being bankrolled by a few rich individuals. Mr Burnham has registered £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,000 from billionaire Lord Sainsbury. In comparison, Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne gave Reform UK a single £9m donation in August 2025 – a sum which exceeds the £8m in trade union donations that Labour will get this year.

The timing makes Labour’s retreat baffling. This newspaper’s revelation of Nigel Farage’s undisclosed £5m gift from Mr Harborne in 2024 has turned big money in politics from an abstract concern into a live issue. Reform’s support has fallen markedly in recent months.

Mr Burnham could recover the situation by backing amendments from two Labour MPs. Stella Creasy’s changes, which have cross-party support, start with a £500,000 cap – Mr Burnham’s own figure – before reducing it, while allowing parliament to alter the level. She proposes to exclude trade union political funds, recognising that money aggregated from thousands of members differs fundamentally from a donation controlled by a single billionaire or company. The former represents many individual contributions; the latter concentrated economic power. Unions warn that a cap might restrict their political activity. But Ms Creasy explicitly protects their member-funded campaigning cash. Opponents should explain why that safeguard is inadequate.

Anneliese Dodds, a former Labour cabinet minister, asks the right question: if ministers believe the growth of big money in politics is a risk, why retain the Conservatives’ sharply increased election spending limits? A donations cap limits how much concentrated private wealth can enter party politics; lower expenditure limits reduce how much money parties need to raise in the first place.

Instead of backing these measures, tabled as amendments to the representation of the people bill at next week’s report stage vote, ministers are pressing ahead with elaborate rules governing where political money comes from and how it reaches parties. Yet this year’s Rycroft review, which ministers are responding to, urged parliament, “if it wishes to restore confidence in the political process and to keep big money out of UK politics”, to consider spending limits. Given the scandals of recent years, it is astonishing that Labour is declining to regulate how much political influence any single wealthy donor can purchase.

editorials.title: What five years as Readers Editor at ThePrint taught me
editorials.passage:
It’s been five years, and I hadn’t even noticed. It was only when a colleague jogged my memory that it struck me—I have been Readers’ Editor at ThePrint for five years. I have become so accustomed to logging into the Readers’ Editor mailbox, reading and replying to your mail, that it’s become a second nature to me. Automatic. Reflexive. Like checking the mobile phone each morning. The joy is that the mailbox is always full. Well, almost always. You readers, are great communicators. You like to share your views on every subject—not just issues ThePrint has written about, but also many we haven’t even thought of, such as “One Death and Some Questions”. You’re annoyed with us when we get something wrong or write something that you disagree with; you’re pleased when you approve of what we’ve written. You complain, you compliment, you urge us to write about this and delete that. I want to say a big thank you. For five years of feedback. For holding up the mirror to our content. For being watchful, alert, and understanding of our limitations. And for the applause. However, more than the praise, which of course we enjoy, thank you for being critical readers of ThePrint, most of all for constantly arguing with us. Keep it coming. While reading some readers’ diatribes against ThePrint—or criticism of my replies to you—I can honestly say I’ve never felt the urge to respond angrily. On the contrary, I welcome it. It makes us at ThePrint think. It makes us revisit the principles of good journalism, the editorial direction we have taken, and the fact that the scales must always be balanced. As Readers Editor, I thank you for keeping this feedback channel alive and happening. I couldn’t have gotten through the last five years without you. You have been my constant companion, and I’m happy in the company I keep. Seriously: It would have been extremely disheartening to log in to the Readers’ Editor mailbox and find that I’ve got no mail. An empty mailbox indicates indifference – that’s the last response ThePrint wants from you. As I wrote in 2023, “Scold us to your heart’s content, berate us, eat us for breakfast — but do stay in touch.” A privilege and a responsibility This anniversary gives me a chance to share with you what I’ve learnt in these five years as Readers’ Editor. A lot. First, to respect the reader. To take your views seriously. In practical terms, that means I must read all mail that lands in the mailbox, and I must reply to all of you, even if it is to say ‘No’. I must share your views with ThePrint team—I am acutely aware that this is a two-way communication, not a one-way street. I believe I have faithfully replied to each one of you who’s written to me. If I missed out on some, forgive the lapse. It wasn’t intentional. The second lesson is one in humility. Over the last 60 months, I have understood that being Readers’ Editor is a privilege. A responsibility. It’s also demanding—you demand accountability from us. That’s partly why I was appointed as Readers’ Editor in July 2021. Six months into being Readers’ Editor, I did reflect upon how I defined my role. In December that year, I wrote, “I see the Readers’ Editor as someone who tries to explain ThePrint to its readers and vice versa, someone who builds bridges between the two, as well as someone who takes her colleagues to task when necessary. There have been times when I haven’t agreed with a reader’s comments but that is because I have felt it was unjustified, not because I feel obliged to blindly defend the website.’’ I do see myself as a bridge that connects readers and ThePrint – a sort of human wi-fi system for them. Especially when you write to the Readers’ Editor because you felt strongly about a matter—and you expect a reply. You trust me to share your views with members of ThePrint team. I do that – and more. Every three months, I try to devote a Readers’ Editor column to readers mail to me. I share as many as I can. Here’s one example—Complaints, corrections, compliments – What ThePrint readers write in about. When you submit articles, which many of you do more frequently every year, you hope we will say ‘Yes’ and publish them. When we don’t, you wait for a reply. I do just that. Usually I write, “Thank you for thinking of ThePrint, but we cannot publish your piece,” and many of you reply graciously, “Thank you so much for your prompt reply.” No hard feelings. In December 2025, one reader rightly called me out and reminded me that I must respect each reader and always be respectful in my replies. We rejected his submitted article, and he wrote, “This submission was met with a curt, one-line dismissal: ‘We do not entertain unsolicited articles’.” That was me. I apologised and have been careful to never repeat the mistake of being “curt”. Above all, you depend on me to initiate action when necessary on your behalf. When you point out genuine factual or grammatical errors, you trust me to pass them on and ensure that they are corrected. I think ThePrint has promptly acted on all such complaints. When you object to reports or opinion articles – which happens regularly – you want me to share them with the writers. And you know what? The writers have often written back with their clarifications. The third lesson I’ve learnt is to be honest. My responsibility is not to blindly defend ThePrint. It is to be fair to readers and to ThePrint. It is to admit we are wrong – publicly. In the monthly Readers Editor column, I try to ensure that. When we mistakenly published an article on an alleged statement by former Bangladesh President Sheikh Hasina before she fled Dhaka in August 2024, and another which incorrectly claimed that “150 gm of semen” was found in the private parts of the rape and murder victim at the RG Kar Medical College and Hospital, Kolkata, both were removed from ThePrint website. I wrote about both in this Readers Editor column. Building a bridge The fourth learning is to fulfil the objectives I wrote about when I became Readers’ Editor. To ‘build a bridge’ between ThePrint and readers. I’ve tried to explain ThePrint to readers. I believe that if I explain how we function, how we create and produce editorial content, and the challenges we face, the readers will gain an understanding of our approach to journalism. I saw no point in writing reams on the principles of good journalism practices. I wanted to show, not tell, with examples from ThePrint’s work. Over the last five years, I have tried to introduce you to ThePrint, the teams that run different departments—from marketing to the various editorial sections and the stories they write or shoot. For example, one Readers’ Editor column covered what goes behind the scenes to produce the explanatory video, Cut the Clutter, five days a week, or why we write a 50-word edit. Other columns described the editing desks, the graphics team, the video and photography departments, the science reporters, the feature writers, the speed desk, etc. I’ve tried to explain how journalists went about their work – often in difficult circumstances, put faces to bylines: Covid pandemic, the Sri Lankan economic crisis (2019), the violence in Manipur, Pahalgam-Operation Sindoor, Air India crash in Ahmedabad, Delhi car blast, general and state elections, Nepal students uprising, the Jantar Mantar protests and other important coverage from August 2021 to August 2026. Complaints, complaints, complaints The fifth lesson in my education as Readers’ Editor has been to keep a level head, to be calm, patient and, when necessary, firm but polite. Over the years, the mailbox has been filled with hatred and venom. Messages also had communal content. By 2026, these are fewer and further between. Between 2021 and 2023, readers regularly shared views about ThePrint’s coverage – and especially its opinion articles—through a Hindu-Muslim bias. Mail often accused ThePrint of being biased. Here is what I wrote in December 2022, “I receive frequent emails accusing ThePrint of “anti-Hindu bias”, of “peddling fake narratives” or “paid news” — “your newspaper (sic) is biased, period”, wrote one aggrieved reader…’’ The common thread in these reproaches is that ThePrint does not give adequate space to the Right but promotes “anti-Hindu” sentiment. That we were sympathetic to the left-liberals. This accusation is unfair and untrue. Repeatedly, I wrote back to readers pointing out that all views were being given space and that ThePrint had no agenda –except to be balanced, fair, and reflect different shades of opinion. I pointed out that we had columnists like R Rajagopalan, Seshadri Chari, Jaithirth Rao whose views “inflect to the right”. This fell on deaf ears of some readers who would reply in uncomplimentary language. As Readers Editor, I learnt to keep my cool, not to reply unkindly, not to be aggressive, or to get into an argument. If readers were determined in their points of view, then so be it. Usually I write, “Thank you for thinking of ThePrint, but we cannot publish your piece,” and many of you reply graciously, “Thank you so much for your prompt reply.” No hard feelings. When you point out genuine factual or grammatical errors, you trust me to pass them on and ensure that they are corrected. I think ThePrint has promptly acted on all such complaints. When you object to reports or opinion articles – which happens regularly – you want me to share them with the writers. And you know what? Repeatedly, I wrote back to readers pointing out that all views were being given space and that ThePrint had no agenda –except to be balanced, fair, and reflect different shades of opinion. This fell on deaf ears of some readers who would reply in uncomplimentary language. As Readers Editor, I learnt to keep my cool, not to reply unkindly, not to be aggressive, or to get into an argument. If readers were determined in their points of view, then so be it. As I often wrote to them, “Everyone is entitled to their views”– the readers too. Usually, this ended the exchange of emails. Another area of regular distress is the pop-up advertisement which accompanies articles. Readers complain that they can’t read the articles because ‘those creatures’ obscure them. I have agreed with them but calmly tried to explain that we cannot stop pop-up ads simply because they are irritating. ThePrint, like any other news media organisation, needs them for financial support. That ends the argument but not the complaints! Ditto with submissions. In the last two years, I have received a constant stream of articles for publication in ThePrint. It is wonderful that so many readers wish to see their name in ThePrint, but it’s impossible to accommodate them all. More often than not, I have to refuse. I have dealt with it extensively in this Readers Editor: Readers have the last word at ThePrint. Keep sending us your mail. However, some readers can be persistent: They repeatedly mail articles and want to know how to improve their writing, topic-selection – and could I please help them? I take a deep breath and recall when I started out in journalism. I too sent articles into publications. I wanted to see my byline. So, I reply to the readers’ mail with writing briefs. On the other hand, ThePrint colleagues are occasionally lax in replying to readers’ mail on their stories. Once again, I had to firmly remind them to do so. My colleagues are usually obliging but sometimes I have to constantly remind them to make a correction or to reply to a mail. Again, patience thy name is Shailaja. That’s it then. As Readers’ Editor, I have other takeaways but we’ll keep those for another column. The Readers Editor’s mission? To listen, learn, and locate ThePrint at the heart of conversations in the news and with its readers. Bring on another year. Shailaja Bajpai is ThePrint’s Readers’ Editor. Over the last five years, I have tried to introduce you to ThePrint, the teams that run different departments—from marketing to the various editorial sections and the stories they write or shoot. For example, one Readers’ Editor column covered what goes behind the scenes to produce the explanatory video, Cut the Clutter, five days a week, or why we write a 50-word edit. Other columns described the editing desks, the graphics team, the video and photography departments, the science reporters, the feature writers, the speed desk, etc. I’ve tried to explain how journalists went about their work – often in difficult circumstances, put faces to bylines: Covid pandemic, the Sri Lankan economic crisis (2019), the violence in Manipur, Pahalgam-Operation Sindoor, Air India crash in Ahmedabad, Delhi car blast, general and state elections, Nepal students uprising, the Jantar Mantar protests and other important coverage from August 2021 to August 2026. Usually I write, “Thank you for thinking of ThePrint, but we cannot publish your piece,” and many of you reply graciously, “Thank you so much for your prompt reply.” No hard feelings. I apologised and have been careful to never repeat the mistake of being “curt”. Above all, you depend on me to initiate action when necessary on your behalf. When you point out genuine factual or grammatical errors, you trust me to pass them on and ensure that they are corrected. I think ThePrint has promptly acted on all such complaints. When you object to reports or opinion articles – which happens regularly – you want me to share them with the writers. And you know what? I believe that if I explain how we function, how we create and produce editorial content, and the challenges we face, the readers will gain an understanding of our approach to journalism. Over the last five years, I have tried to introduce you to ThePrint, the teams that run different departments—from marketing to the various editorial sections and the stories they write or shoot. For example, one Readers’ Editor column covered what goes behind the scenes to produce the explanatory video, Cut the Clutter, five days a week, or why we write a 50-word edit. Other columns described the editing desks, the graphics team, the video and photography departments, the science reporters, the feature writers, the speed desk, etc. I’ve tried to explain how journalists went about their work – often in difficult circumstances, put faces to bylines: Covid pandemic, the Sri Lankan economic crisis (2019), the violence in Manipur, Pahalgam-Operation Sindoor, Air India crash in Ahmedabad, Delhi car blast, general and state elections, Nepal students uprising, the Jantar Mantar protests and other important coverage from August 2021 to August 2026. Over the years, the mailbox has been filled with hatred and venom. Messages also had communal content. By 2026, these are fewer and further between. Between 2021 and 2023, readers regularly shared views about ThePrint’s coverage – and especially its opinion articles—through a Hindu-Muslim bias. Mail often accused ThePrint of being biased. Here is what I wrote in December 2022, “I receive frequent emails accusing ThePrint of “anti-Hindu bias”, of “peddling fake narratives” or “paid news” — “your newspaper (sic) is biased, period”, wrote one aggrieved reader…’’ The common thread in these reproaches is that ThePrint does not give adequate space to the Right but promotes “anti-Hindu” sentiment. That we were sympathetic to the left-liberals. This accusation is unfair and untrue. Repeatedly, I wrote back to readers pointing out that all views were being given space and that ThePrint had no agenda –except to be balanced, fair, and reflect different shades of opinion. I pointed out that we had columnists like R Rajagopalan, Seshadri Chari, Jaithirth Rao whose views “inflect to the right”. This fell on deaf ears of some readers who would reply in uncomplimentary language. As I often wrote to them, “Everyone is entitled to their views”– the readers too. Usually, this ended the exchange of emails. Another area of regular distress is the pop-up advertisement which accompanies articles. Readers complain that they can’t read the articles because ‘those creatures’ obscure them. I have agreed with them but calmly tried to explain that we cannot stop pop-up ads simply because they are irritating. ThePrint, like any other news media organisation, needs them for financial support. That ends the argument but not the complaints! Ditto with submissions. In the last two years, I have received a constant stream of articles for publication in ThePrint. I take a deep breath and recall when I started out in journalism. I too sent articles into publications. I wanted to see my byline. So, I reply to the readers’ mail with writing briefs. On the other hand, ThePrint colleagues are occasionally lax in replying to readers’ mail on their stories. Once again, I had to firmly remind them to do so. My colleagues are usually obliging but sometimes I have to constantly remind them to make a correction or to reply to a mail. Again, patience thy name is Shailaja. That’s it then. As Readers’ Editor, I have other takeaways but we’ll keep those for another column. The Readers Editor’s mission? To listen, learn, and locate ThePrint at the heart of conversations in the news and with its readers. Bring on another year. Shailaja Bajpai is ThePrint’s Readers’ Editor. Between 2021 and 2023, readers regularly shared views about ThePrint’s coverage – and especially its opinion articles—through a Hindu-Muslim bias. Mail often accused ThePrint of being biased. Here is what I wrote in December 2022, “I receive frequent emails accusing ThePrint of “anti-Hindu bias”, of “peddling fake narratives” or “paid news” — “your newspaper (sic) is biased, period”, wrote one aggrieved reader…’’ The common thread in these reproaches is that ThePrint does not give adequate space to the Right but promotes “anti-Hindu” sentiment. That we were sympathetic to the left-liberals. This accusation is unfair and untrue. Repeatedly, I wrote back to readers pointing out that all views were being given space and that ThePrint had no agenda –except to be balanced, fair, and reflect different shades of opinion. I pointed out that we had columnists like R Rajagopalan, Seshadri Chari, Jaithirth Rao whose views “inflect to the right”. This fell on deaf ears of some readers who would reply in uncomplimentary language. As Readers Editor, I learnt to keep my cool, not to reply unkindly, not to be aggressive, or to get into an argument. If readers were determined in their points of view, then so be it. As I often wrote to them, “Everyone is entitled to their views”– the readers too. Usually, this ended the exchange of emails. Another area of regular distress is the pop-up advertisement which accompanies articles. Readers complain that they can’t read the articles because ‘those creatures’ obscure them. I have agreed with them but calmly tried to explain that we cannot stop pop-up ads simply because they are irritating. ThePrint, like any other news media organisation, needs them for financial support. That ends the argument but not the complaints! Ditto with submissions. In the last two years, I have received a constant stream of articles for publication in ThePrint. It is wonderful that so many readers wish to see their name in ThePrint, but it’s impossible to accommodate them all. More often than not, I have to refuse. I have dealt with it extensively in this Readers Editor: Readers have the last word at ThePrint. Keep sending us your mail. However, some readers can be persistent: They repeatedly mail articles and want to know how to improve their writing, topic-selection – and could I please help them? I take a deep breath and recall when I started out in journalism. I too sent articles into publications. I wanted to see my byline. So, I reply to the readers’ mail with writing briefs. On the other hand, ThePrint colleagues are occasionally lax in replying to readers’ mail on their stories. Once again, I had to firmly remind them to do so. My colleagues are usually obliging but sometimes I have to constantly remind them to make a correction or to reply to a mail. Again, patience thy name is Shailaja. That’s it then. As Readers’ Editor, I have other takeaways but we’ll keep those for another column. The Readers Editor’s mission? To listen, learn, and locate ThePrint at the heart of conversations in the news and with its readers. Bring on another year. Shailaja Bajpai is ThePrint’s Readers’ Editor.
